mood.p: Zondag 6 september wordt een echte nazomerdag. Na een frisse nacht van 7 tot 11 graden voert een zuidoostenwind warme lucht aan en loopt het kwik op naar 21 graden in het noorden tot 24 in het zuiden, met zon, wolkenvelden en vrijwel overal droog weer. Maandag wordt het 23 tot 27 graden, maar dinsdag draait de wind naar het westen en woensdag, de dag van de landelijke ov-staking, is het wisselvallig met buien en zo'n 16 graden. De stemming in het land is gemengd. Ipsos I&O meet een record van 70 procent ontevreden kiezers over het kabinet-Jetten, negen dagen voor Prinsjesdag. Het geweld in Overasselt en de twee doden bij een bedrijfsongeval in Zwaag drukken op het gemoed, terwijl families van vermiste Nederlanders in Nepal nog wachten op nieuws. Voetbalfans hadden zaterdagavond wel iets te vieren of te betreuren: PSV won de topper in Amsterdam met 3-1 van Ajax. Voor velen is dit het weekend voor een laatste terrasje voordat de herfst zich meldt.

global.h3: US destroys three Iranian tankers after missiles fired at Navy warships
global.summary: CENTCOM said on 5 September it disabled two Iranian crude carriers and destroyed a third after the Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer in the Gulf.
body: US Central Command reported on Saturday 5 September that its forces had permanently disabled the tankers Downy, off Kharg Island, and Stark 1, near Jask, and destroyed the Kylo in the Gulf of Oman. The action came hours after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles toward an American aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, both of which evaded the attacks without casualties.

CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper framed the response as a deliberate exchange rate, warning that firing on two US ships would cost Iran three of its own and that Washington would destroy Iran's exposed oil fleet if necessary. Iran's military command replied that its strikes on US vessels would become more severe and could expand. The confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz has continued despite a ceasefire memorandum signed in June.

global.h3: Trump calls Iran conflict 'small potatoes' as Vance says it is not a war
global.summary: The president said on 4 September that the US has essentially taken over Iran, a day after his vice president refused to call the six-month conflict a war.
body: Speaking at the White House on Friday 4 September, President Trump dismissed the Iran conflict as small potatoes and said it did not matter whether it was labelled a war or a military conflict. He backed Vice President JD Vance, who told reporters on Thursday that major combat operations had lasted only six weeks and that there was no active shooting at the moment.

The Pentagon's casualty database now lists 767 US troops wounded since strikes began on 28 February, up from 758 on 28 August. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei accused Washington of deliberately hitting civilian targets including schools, hospitals and a wedding, an incident Vance said was being investigated while he expressed scepticism about Iranian claims.

global.h3: Putin orders 72-hour pause on Kyiv strikes as US envoys land in Moscow
global.summary: The Kremlin announced a three-day halt to attacks on Kyiv from midnight Saturday, hours after Russian missiles and about 167 drones hit the city's two airports.
body: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived at Moscow's Vnukovo airport on Saturday 5 September, met by Kremlin negotiator Kirill Dmitriev, carrying what President Trump has called a fresh concrete proposal to end the war. Shortly afterwards the Kremlin said Vladimir Putin had ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv, tied to the envoys' planned visit to the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.

The pause followed one of the heaviest nights in months. A Russian drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service in central Kyiv on Friday afternoon, the first hit on that building in the war, and an overnight barrage targeted Boryspil and Zhuliany airports, killing at least seven people nationwide. Zelensky called the airport strikes deliberate and had earlier offered a reciprocal halt to Ukrainian long-range strikes for the duration of the visit.

global.h3: Zelensky approves retaliation plans and promises to pick the moment
global.summary: Ukraine's president said on 4 September he had signed off on SBU and military proposals to answer Russian strikes on cities, while Trump blamed stalled talks on personal animosity.
body: In his evening address on Friday 4 September, Volodymyr Zelensky said he had approved proposals from the Security Service and the Armed Forces for responses to Russia's continuing attacks on Ukrainian cities, adding that Kyiv would choose its own time to act. The statement came as a Russian strike set fire to the roof of a nine-storey apartment block in Boryspil, 29 kilometres east of Kyiv, injuring two women.

At a White House press conference the same day, President Trump confirmed that Witkoff and Kushner would visit both Moscow and Kyiv and attributed the diplomatic stalemate to bad blood between Zelensky and Putin. Ukraine's General Staff put Russian losses at 1,495,050 troops since February 2022, including 1,260 in the past day.

global.h3: Ukraine anti-graft agencies raid Prosecutor General's office
global.summary: NABU and SAPO searched premises linked to a deputy prosecutor general and the Odesa governor on 4 September, targeting an alleged criminal organisation inside the prosecution service.
body: Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office launched a large operation at the Prosecutor General's Office on Friday 4 September. The agencies said they were investigating an alleged criminal organisation headed by an official of the office, with searches reported at addresses tied to a deputy prosecutor general and to the governor of Odesa Oblast.

The Prosecutor General's Office denied that Ruslan Kravchenko himself had been searched. The raids land at a sensitive moment, with US envoys due in Kyiv on Sunday and Western partners watching Ukraine's handling of corruption cases as a condition for continued support and EU accession progress.

global.h3: Memorial chief warns Russia will jail more people after September vote
global.summary: Elena Zhemkova told AFP in Amsterdam that repression could intensify sharply after Russia's legislative elections, with more detainees sent to fight in Ukraine.
body: The executive director of Memorial, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning rights group outlawed in Russia, said she fears a new crackdown once the September Duma elections are out of the way. Speaking to AFP in Amsterdam, where she now lives in exile, Zhemkova said more people were likely to be arrested and pushed to the front in Ukraine.

Memorial was liquidated by Russian courts in late 2021 and later declared illegal, but Zhemkova said the organisation would keep documenting political prisoners from abroad. Her warning comes as the Kremlin negotiates with US envoys while simultaneously escalating air attacks on Ukrainian cities.

global.h3: AfD on the brink of a first far-right state win in Saxony-Anhalt
global.summary: Voters in the eastern German state go to the polls on Sunday 6 September with the AfD polling around 40 to 42 percent, roughly double the governing CDU.
body: Saxony-Anhalt elects a new state parliament on Sunday with Alternative fuer Deutschland projected at 41 to 42 percent by Infratest dimap, far ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU at about 23 percent. The AfD's 35-year-old lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund has built a TikTok following close to the size of the state's electorate, while CDU incumbent Sven Schulze has only held the minister-presidency since January.

Every mainstream party maintains a firewall against governing with the AfD, so even a clear plurality would not hand Siegmund power outright and could instead leave the state unable to form a government. Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern vote in two weeks with the AfD leading or close to leading in both, making Sunday's result a template the party hopes to repeat.

global.h3: Belgrade honours Mladic without state ceremony as EU commissioner stays away
global.summary: A commemoration for the convicted Srebrenica genocide commander was held on 5 September at the Home of the Army of Serbia, while Marta Kos cancelled her Serbia trip.
body: Ratko Mladic, who died in UN custody in The Hague on 27 August at 84, was commemorated on Saturday 5 September at the Home of the Army of Serbia in central Belgrade, organised by an association of retired generals. President Aleksandar Vucic said there would be no state or military honours and that he would not attend, citing a long-scheduled visit by the president of Uzbekistan. Burial follows on Monday.

EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos scrapped a planned Belgrade visit, saying the glorification around Mladic's death is incompatible with the values underpinning Serbia's EU path and calling the funeral an important test. Vucic dismissed the criticism as stupid. UEFA had already fined Red Star Belgrade for fan chants honouring Mladic days earlier.

global.h3: Five EU states, including the Netherlands, push 'return hubs' deal for 2027
global.summary: Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands want to send rejected asylum seekers to hubs outside the EU by 2027 but have not named a host country.
body: The five governments are working toward a joint agreement to deport migrants who exhaust their asylum claims to processing and removal centres in partner countries outside the European Union. German interior minister Alexander Dobrindt said he aims to sign with a host nation this year, and Denmark's Morten Bodskov expects a common understanding around the new year. The group reconvenes in Munich later in September.

No candidate host has been publicly identified. The Council of Europe has warned the model carries considerable human rights risks, and the Danish Refugee Council argues hubs will not stop irregular routes such as the Ceuta crossing that Spain is still investigating. For the Dutch cabinet the plan is a chance to show progress on migration ahead of Prinsjesdag.

global.h3: Trump says Europe must repay 'hundreds of billions' in Ukraine aid
global.summary: In a Truth Social post this week the president said Washington would seek reimbursement from European governments for aid sent under Biden, naming no country or mechanism.
body: Donald Trump wrote that the United States would be asking European governments, somewhat belatedly, to repay hundreds of billions of dollars in assistance sent to Ukraine and NATO during the Biden administration. He gave no figure per country and no legal route, but the demand landed in the same week his envoys flew to Moscow to seek a peace deal.

European capitals have not responded on the record, partly because the request lacks specifics. Estimates of total US aid to Ukraine since 2022 range from Kyiv's count of roughly 100 billion dollars to the far larger and disputed numbers Trump has cited before. Finance ministries describe the mood as fatigue rather than defiance.

global.h3: Canada's C$27.6 billion retaliatory tariffs bite on Monday with no talks
global.summary: Ottawa's counter-tariffs on US steel, aluminium and about 700 other products take effect on 8 September, two weeks after negotiations collapsed.
body: Canada's retaliatory package, announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney on 22 August after trade talks with Washington broke down, takes effect on Monday 8 September. It doubles tariffs on American steel and aluminium to 50 percent and adds duties on roughly 700 goods from dairy and appliances to pulp, paper and electronics, matching the 50 percent US levies dollar for dollar.

Nothing reported this week suggests the negotiations have resumed. Carney complained the American position had softened only in tone, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick accused Ottawa of playing politics. Mexico is watching closely, with the fourth round of USMCA automotive talks opening this month.

global.h3: Pentagon holds free 35 percent stake in Venezuela oil venture, reports show
global.summary: Details of the 1 September deal granting 100-year rights to 65 billion barrels reveal the Office of Strategic Capital as a no-cost equity partner. Senator Reed called it an abuse of power.
body: The agreement signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on 1 September gives North American Blue Energy Partners, owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, century-long rights over 17 fields. Reporting this week showed the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital holds 35 percent of the firm at no cost, while the State Department can buy a fifth of output at cost, free of Venezuelan tax, with a veto over board seats.

Senator Jack Reed, top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said the arrangement turns the US military into an investor in Venezuelan oil and abuses taxpayer dollars. Opposition figures around Maria Corina Machado object that an unelected government in Caracas has signed away a resource no future elected one may be able to reclaim.

global.h3: Strong US jobs report lifts odds of a Fed rate hike, stocks slip
global.summary: Employers added 162,000 jobs in August against forecasts of 55,000, pushing the 10-year yield to 4.789 percent and the S&P 500 down 0.38 percent to 7,719.
body: The August payrolls report released on Friday 4 September showed 162,000 new jobs, nearly three times the consensus, with unemployment steady at 4.1 percent. Traders now price roughly even odds that the Federal Reserve raises rates at its meeting this month, a sharp turn from expectations of further cuts only weeks ago.

The S&P 500 fell to 7,719, the Dow lost 0.51 percent to 53,414 and the Nasdaq slipped 0.29 percent to 26,507. The dollar index rose to 99.157 and gold dropped 1.14 percent to 4,429 dollars an ounce. Next week's US consumer price index is the next test, with OPEC meeting on Saturday and Brent closing the week at 96.28 dollars.

global.h3: US diesel hits record 5.85 dollars as Gulf strikes push Brent to 96
global.summary: AAA's national diesel average passed the June 2022 record on 4 September while regular petrol averaged 4.15 dollars, nearly a dollar above a year ago.
body: AAA reported a national average diesel price of 5.85 dollars a gallon on Friday, edging past the 5.82 dollar record set in June 2022, as Brent crude closed the week at 96.28 dollars, its highest since 24 July. Regular petrol averaged 4.15 dollars against 3.20 a year earlier, even as the TSA expected to screen more than 17 million passengers over the Labor Day travel period.

Vice President Vance said prices could have been much higher without the administration's efforts but would not say whether 3-dollar petrol remains a promise. Democratic Senator Mark Kelly warned that diesel costs feed straight into grocery bills through farms and freight, a politically sensitive line in a midterm year.

global.h3: Nepal glacier disaster toll reaches 1,342 dead with nearly 4,900 missing
global.summary: Police in Nepal confirmed 1,342 deaths as of Saturday morning from the 26 August Langtang Lirung collapse, as scientists say the failure was decades in the making.
body: A section of the Langtang Lirung glacier gave way above Rasuwa district on 26 August, sending a wall of ice, rock and water some 100 kilometres down the Trishuli valley into Tibet. Nepal's police put confirmed deaths at 1,342 as of the morning of 5 September, with nearly 4,900 people still missing, among them hundreds of foreign trekkers and pilgrims. Chinese authorities have confirmed 21 deaths and 541 missing on the Tibetan side.

The surge buried whole villages, blocked hydropower tunnels, destroyed bridges and swept away the Gyirong border port. The UN Development Programme estimates at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris. Scientists told reporters the glacier had been destabilising for decades as the Himalayas warm, and a CNN report found warning signs were visible before the collapse.

global.h3: World food prices climb to highest level since 2022, FAO says
global.summary: The FAO Food Price Index averaged 133.3 points in August, up from 130.8 in July, as Black Sea strikes, European drought and El Nino fears pushed grains to three-year highs.
body: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization reported on 4 September that its index rose to 133.3 points in August, the highest reading since late 2022 though still about 17 percent below the March 2022 peak that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Cereals, vegetable oils, sugar, meat and dairy all rose, with grains up 2.5 points on uncertainty over Black Sea export flows.

Sugar jumped 11.9 percent to its highest since June 2025 on weaker output in Brazil's centre-south. The FAO cited extreme heat and drought in Europe, the risk of a severe El Nino and trade disruption from the Ukraine and Iran wars. Corn futures surged 10 percent on Friday alone.

global.h3: Alberta referendum ballots arrive incomplete as 290,000 request mail votes
global.summary: Elections Alberta confirmed some packages mailed from 1 September were missing questions and moved its application deadline forward to 25 September.
body: Elections Alberta said this week that some special ballot packages for the 19 October referendum arrived without one or more of the ten questions voters must answer, including the question on separation from Canada. Deputy chief electoral officer Dallas Stoesz said the glued packages separated in transit like notepads. Roughly 290,000 mail-ballot applications, an unprecedented volume, forced the agency to bring its deadline forward two weeks.

Officials plan to count all ten questions by hand under a strict 48-hour rule, with the separation question tallied first and results not expected before 1 to 4 am on 20 October. The episode adds administrative strain to a vote already testing Canada's unity during a trade war with Washington.

netherlands.h3: Record 70 percent of voters dissatisfied with Jetten cabinet before Prinsjesdag
netherlands.summary: An Ipsos I&O poll published 5 September puts dissatisfaction at 70 percent, up from 63 in July, with only 18 percent approving the cabinet's policies ten days before the budget.
body: Satisfaction with the Jetten I cabinet has fallen to its lowest point since Rob Jetten took office in February, according to Ipsos I&O. Seventy percent of voters are now dissatisfied, against 63 percent in July, and only 9 percent believe the government can solve the country's problems. Researchers blame the drawn-out budget negotiations, which produced a deal the coalition still cannot pass without opposition votes in either chamber.

Support has slipped across the coalition, with just over half of D66 voters, 43 percent of CDA voters and 23 percent of VVD voters still satisfied. If elections were held now, PRO would become the largest party with a projected 26 seats, matching what D66 and VVD each won last year, while D66 would fall to 20 and VVD to 17. JA21 and Forum voor Democratie would gain.

netherlands.h3: Public officials among thousands posting homophobic abuse at Jetten
netherlands.summary: An AD analysis of 45,860 replies to the prime minister's X posts found 2,293 homophobic responses, with a council official, a police employee and an air force member among repeat posters.
body: The Algemeen Dagblad analysed replies to 323 posts from Rob Jetten's official account during his first six months in office and found one in 20 was homophobic. The abuse appeared under routine messages, from congratulations to Queen Maxima to a post on Amsterdam Pride, and mostly took the form of a single insinuating question repeated hundreds of times rather than open slurs.

Most accounts left one reply and never returned, and the ten most persistent produced under 6 percent of the total. Leiden criminal law professor Marloes van Noorloos said the insinuations are hard to prosecute as hate speech, though civil servants could face disciplinary action. Jetten, the country's first openly gay prime minister, files a police report every week and has accused platforms of barely moderating hate.

netherlands.h3: Defence blacklists Polarsteps after app exposed soldiers' locations
netherlands.summary: Follow the Money found dozens of Dutch service members could be tracked to bases and missions abroad through the travel app, with home addresses sometimes exposed.
body: Investigative platform Follow the Money reported on 5 September that GPS data leaking from the back end of the social travel app Polarsteps allowed it to trace dozens of Dutch military personnel to bases at home and deployments abroad, and in some cases to their home addresses. The Ministry of Defence blacklisted the app as soon as it received questions from the journalists.

The platform said it could retrieve names, hometowns, follower lists, photos and GPS tracks for around 23 million users worldwide through the app's API. Experts warned foreign intelligence services could use such data to map troop movements or blackmail individuals. According to Follow the Money, Polarsteps CEO Clare Jones acknowledged the company had known about the exposure since at least December 2025.

netherlands.h3: Farmers still face 5 to 10 percent livestock cut as nitrogen plan falls short
netherlands.summary: PBL found the 20 billion euro nitrogen package would just miss its 2035 target. Minister Van Essen called a blanket cut an emergency brake the cabinet will not use.
body: The environmental assessment agency PBL reviewed the cabinet's nitrogen plan at the government's request and called it an important step, but concluded the measures worked out so far leave a gap. Closing it would still require an across-the-board reduction of 5 to 10 percent in livestock rights, the permits that cap how many animals a farm may keep.

Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen said on Friday that a compulsory cut is a no-go and only a last resort if targets are missed in 2035. Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42 to 46 percent against 2019 levels under the June package. PBL expects herds to shrink anyway and some farms to close, while BBB and farm lobby LTO called the extra cut unacceptable.

netherlands.h3: Nationwide public transport strike on Wednesday goes ahead
netherlands.summary: FNV confirmed the 24-hour stoppage at NS, regional and city transport on 9 September after the cabinet declined to drop welfare cuts, six days before Prinsjesdag.
body: Workers across Dutch public transport and the rail sector will down tools for 24 hours on Wednesday 9 September. The FNV union says the action is a signal to the minority Jetten cabinet against planned cuts to social security, under the slogan Stop de afbraak van onze sociale zekerheid. Travel planner 9292 and NS are warning passengers to expect almost no service that day.

The strike follows a port workers' stoppage on Friday and is part of a series of actions the unions are building toward Prinsjesdag on 15 September. The Raad van State said court hearings will proceed as scheduled despite the disruption. Weather forecasters expect a wet and windy day, adding to the incentive to work from home.

netherlands.h3: Rents up 4.4 percent in July, Rotterdam sees steepest big-city rise
netherlands.summary: CBS figures show a slower increase than the 4.9 percent of 2025 and 5.4 percent of 2024, with sitting tenants paying 3.8 percent more and new lets rising faster.
body: Rents rose an average 4.4 percent in July compared with a year earlier, the national statistics office reported, the third consecutive year of increases above 4 percent but the smallest of the three. Tenants who stayed put saw a 3.8 percent rise, while rents jumped more sharply when homes were re-let to new occupants.

Among the four big cities Rotterdam recorded 4.7 percent, Utrecht 4.5, The Hague 4.4 and Amsterdam 4.3. Overijssel and Noord-Brabant led the provinces at 4.6 percent and Friesland trailed at 4 percent. The social housing cap this year is 4.1 percent, but re-lets and income-based surcharges of 50 or 100 euros a month can push rents higher.

netherlands.h3: Free 0800 hotline opens for people stuck with tax and benefits problems
netherlands.summary: The line, run by help platform Geldfit on weekdays from 9 am to 9 pm, is aimed at citizens who cannot resolve complex cases with the Belastingdienst or Toeslagen on their own.
body: People who hit a wall with the Tax Authority or the Benefits Agency can now call a free 0800 number, NL Times reported on 5 September. Operators at Geldfit assess what each caller needs and route them to the right help. Taxpayer advocate Hayde Zarkeshan told NU.nl that her office knows exactly where people get stuck trying to access legal tax aid.

The advocate's post was created in the aftermath of the childcare benefits scandal and has handled hundreds of cases since 2025. The launch comes in the same week the government moved to restrict free legal aid for benefits scandal victims in disputes with municipalities. Complex cases can also still go to the Tax Administration's Stella team.

netherlands.h3: UK airport data leak hits thousands of Dutch travellers
netherlands.summary: BNR identified Dutch victims in a dark web dump of around 9 million Manchester Airports Group records, which may include the Dutch-born wife of British PM Andy Burnham.
body: Personal data of thousands of Dutch travellers who passed through Manchester, London Stansted or East Midlands airports was published on the dark web earlier this week, NL Times reported on 5 September. News platform BNR traced the Dutch records in a leak affecting roughly 9 million people, a figure it said is probably an undercount.

BNR said records belonging to Prime Minister Andy Burnham could be identified with certainty and that entries pointing to his wife Marie-France van Heel contained no highly sensitive fields, so her inclusion cannot be confirmed. The breach adds to a run of data stories in the Netherlands, including an Amsterdam travel app that leaked users' details for months.

netherlands.h3: Second worker dies after chemical accident at Zwaag industrial site
netherlands.summary: A 40-year-old man died on Friday 5 September hours after a colleague, following reports that the two fell into a vat of chemicals at a Noord-Holland firm.
body: Emergency services were called to an industrial estate in Zwaag at about 9.45 am on Friday 4 September and found two workers who had to be resuscitated after contact with a hazardous substance. One died that morning and the second, a 40-year-old man, died later on Friday, AD reported. Two trauma helicopters were deployed and the area was sealed off.

The Labour Inspectorate is investigating and said the report concerned a fall situation, without confirming a relative's account to NU.nl that the men fell into a vat of chemicals. The local safety region said the released substances posed no danger to residents nearby.

netherlands.h3: Ministry colleague among Dutch still missing after Nepal glacier flood
netherlands.summary: Agriculture minister Van Essen told MPs a civil servant from her ministry has been missing since the 26 August disaster, as two Dutch pilgrims also remain unaccounted for.
body: During a Tweede Kamer debate reported on 5 September, minister Jaimi van Essen paused to say that a colleague from the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Food Security and Nature had been travelling in the area when the Langtang Lirung glacier collapsed and has not been heard from since. She described the colleague as someone who pours heart and soul into the nature portfolio.

Three Dutch nationals were reported missing at the end of August. Contact has since been made with a Dutch woman who lives in Nepal, but two people on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet are still missing. Nepal's official toll passed 1,280 on its side of the border, with thousands unaccounted for.

netherlands.h3: At least 49 opinion pieces in Dutch papers were written entirely by AI
netherlands.summary: AI Report analysed 252 recent op-eds in Volkskrant, Trouw, Parool and FD and found 49 fully machine-written and 57 partly so. Volkskrant's editor said he was surprised by the scale.
body: The platform AI Report, run by journalist Alexander Kloepping, examined 252 opinion pieces published last month in major dailies. At least 49 were entirely AI-generated and 57 more were partly so. At de Volkskrant more than a quarter of the pieces were flagged, prompting editor-in-chief Pieter Klok to send contributors a letter banning AI in submitted articles except as a spell-checker.

FD editor Perry Feenstra said the figure made him uncomfortable but noted that people with something to say and weak writing skills are no longer sidelined. Trouw allows AI for translation and copy-editing, while Het Parool called the practice unacceptable. Writers themselves said they used AI to sharpen their ideas and arguments.

netherlands.h3: Dutch soil scientist wins Ig Nobel for burying 1,000 pairs of underpants
netherlands.summary: Marcel van der Heijden of the University of Zurich shared the soil science prize at a ceremony held outside the US for the first time in more than 30 years.
body: Van der Heijden and three colleagues had volunteers in more than 25 countries bury identical cotton underpants and dig them up two months later. The more the fabric had rotted, the healthier and more biologically active the soil, showing that management choices directly affect soil life. The Ig Nobels reward research that first makes people laugh and then makes them think.

This year's ceremony took place in Zurich after organisers said they could not in good conscience ask winners and journalists to travel to the United States, a decision widely read as a response to US immigration policy. Next year's event moves to Antwerp. Dutch researchers have now won 22 Ig Nobels since 1991, including last year's prize for showing a drink improves foreign-language skills.

netherlands.h3: Overasselt: 32 suspects held as wounded officer leaves hospital
netherlands.summary: Prosecutors are holding 32 people, including 16 French nationals, 11 Dutch and two minors, over the 1 September shootout that killed security guard Barry Leenders.
body: A police officer wounded in the fatal Overasselt shooting was released from hospital on 5 September, NL Times reported. The attack on Ewijkseweg on 1 September, captured on security cameras showing dozens of armed and masked men, killed 51-year-old security guard Barry Leenders and injured two officers. Prosecutors have remanded 32 suspects into custody, among them 16 French and 11 Dutch nationals and two minors.

Justice minister David van Weel insisted this week that the Netherlands is not a narco state and vowed to catch a wanted drug trafficker linked to the case. The episode continues to dominate national debate about organised crime days before the cabinet presents its security budget.
